lead: The Laplace transform turns a time signal x(t) into a function X(s) of complex frequency s=σ+jω. It multiplies x(t) by a damping factor e⁻ˢᵗ before integrating, so signals that grow too fast for the Fourier transform can still be handled. The integral converges only for some s values; that set is the region of convergence, ROC. Engineers use it to solve circuits and control problems with differential equations, to read stability from poles, and to design filters. The ROC is as important as X(s): it tells which time signal you actually have.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 standard signals u(t) and exponentials; Unit 3 Fourier transform for the damping idea; properties come later in Chapter 4.2.

blocks.text: Start with a continuous-time signal x(t). The one-sided Laplace transform is defined for t≥0. It is written X(s).

blocks.where: x(t) is the time signal; s=σ+jω is complex frequency; σ is damping in s⁻¹; ω is angular frequency in rad/s; X(s) is the transform.

blocks.text: Write e<sup>−st</sup>=e<sup>−σt</sup>e<sup>−jωt</sup>. The factor e<sup>−jωt</sup> rotates the signal at frequency ω. The factor e<sup>−σt</sup> damps or grows it. The Fourier transform is the special case σ=0. For a causal signal (x(t)=0 for t<0), X(jω)=X(s) at s=jω when the ROC includes the jω axis. The extra σ is why the Laplace transform can handle e<sup>2t</sup>u(t), which has no ordinary Fourier transform.

A bilateral form integrates from −∞ to ∞: X(s)=∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup> x(t)e<sup>−st</sup>dt. The one-sided form is used for causal signals, which are zero for t<0. The left-sided and two-sided examples below state that they use the bilateral form.

sections.h3: Convergence and the region of convergence

blocks.text: The integral is improper. It converges when the limit at ∞ is finite. Test with x(t)=e<sup>−at</sup>u(t), where a is real. Some syllabi call the convergence set the region of convergence.

blocks.where: a is a real decay rate in s⁻¹; the result holds when Re(s+a)>0, that is Re(s)>−a. Re(s) means the real part σ.

blocks.text: That inequality is the ROC. For a=2, X(s)=1/(s+2) and ROC Re(s)>−2. The pole is at s=−2. The ROC is an open half-plane to the right of the pole. It never contains the pole: at s=−2 the integrand becomes e<sup>0t</sup>=1 and the integral diverges.

A left-sided signal gives the same algebra with a different region. Using the bilateral transform, take x(t)=−e<sup>−at</sup>u(−t). Then X(s)=1/(s+a), but the integral converges for Re(s)<−a. The minus sign makes the two time signals different. For a two-sided signal such as x(t)=e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t)+e<sup>3t</sup>u(−t), X(s)=1/(s+2)−1/(s−3) and ROC is −2<Re(s)<3.

For the bilateral transform, poles alone do not fix the signal. X(s)=1/(s+2) can come from e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t) with ROC Re(s)>−2, or from −e<sup>−2t</sup>u(−t) with ROC Re(s)<−2. The ROC chooses the side. A right-sided signal has ROC to the right of its rightmost pole. A left-sided signal has ROC to the left of its leftmost pole. A two-sided signal has a strip between poles.

sections.h3: Reading a transform with its ROC

blocks.text: The table's left-sided and two-sided rows use the bilateral transform.

Check each row by the integral. For row 1, the exponential decays for t≥0. For row 2, the signal is nonzero for t≤0 and the minus sign is part of x(t). For row 3, the first term needs Re(s)>−2 and the second needs Re(s)<3; both must hold, so the ROC is the overlap.

When you meet X(s), factor the denominator to find poles. Mark poles on the s-plane: σ is horizontal, jω is vertical. Use the stated ROC to choose left or right sides. The ROC cannot cross a pole. For a causal system, the ROC is the half-plane to the right of the rightmost pole; stability needs the jω axis inside the ROC. System use is in Chapter 4.4.

examples.question: Find the Laplace transform and ROC of x(t)=e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t). State the pole location.
steps: The unit step u(t) is 0 for t<0 and 1 for t≥0. Thus x(t)=e<sup>−2t</sup> for t≥0 and x(t)=0 for t<0.
Write the one-sided transform: X(s)=∫₀<sup>∞</sup> e<sup>−2t</sup>e<sup>−st</sup>dt.
So Re(s)>−2. The pole is s=−2. The ROC is Re(s)>−2, so the pole is on the boundary and not inside.
examples.answer: X(s)=1/(s+2), pole at s=−2, and ROC Re(s)>−2.

traps: Writing X(s)=1/(s+2) but omitting Re(s)>−2: the transform alone does not identify the time signal.
Putting the pole s=−2 inside the ROC: the ROC is always open and never contains a pole.
Using the right-sided ROC for a left-sided signal: −e<sup>−2t</sup>u(−t) shares 1/(s+2) but has Re(s)<−2.
Treating s as jω only: s=σ+jω; the Fourier transform is the special case σ=0 and only when the ROC includes the jω axis.
Adding transforms without intersecting their ROCs; for a two-sided sum use the bilateral transform and take the overlap strip.

quiz.q: Define the one-sided Laplace transform and the variable s.
quiz.a: X(s)=∫₀<sup>∞</sup> x(t)e<sup>−st</sup>dt, and s=σ+jω is complex frequency.
The ROC is the set of s values for which the defining Laplace integral converges.

quiz.q: Why does the factor e<sup>−σt</sup> help the Laplace transform handle signals that the Fourier transform cannot?
quiz.a: It adds damping e<sup>−σt</sup> before integration. A growing signal can be made to decay fast enough for the integral to converge.

quiz.q: Find the Laplace transform and ROC of x(t)=e<sup>−5t</sup>u(t).
quiz.a: X(s)=1/(s+5), ROC Re(s)>−5. The pole is s=−5 and is not inside the ROC.

quiz.q: A signal has X(s)=1/(s+3) and is left-sided. Give its ROC.
quiz.a: For a left-sided signal with pole at s=−3, the ROC is Re(s)<−3.

quiz.q: Two signals have the same X(s)=1/(s+2). One has ROC Re(s)>−2 and the other has ROC Re(s)<−2. What is the time-domain difference?
quiz.a: ROC Re(s)>−2 gives e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t), a right-sided decaying signal. ROC Re(s)<−2 gives −e<sup>−2t</sup>u(−t), a left-sided signal. Their causality and stability differ; only the first ROC includes the jω axis.

quiz.q: Why can the ROC never contain a pole?
quiz.a: At a pole the transform value is infinite. At that s the defining integral does not converge to a finite number, so the pole is excluded from the ROC.

quiz.q: For x(t)=e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t)+e<sup>3t</sup>u(−t), explain why the ROC is a strip.
quiz.a: Using the bilateral transform, the first term needs Re(s)>−2. The second term needs Re(s)<3. Both conditions must hold, giving the strip −2<Re(s)<3.

beyond: Not for the exam. Laplace's idea grew from operational calculus and is now the language of control and circuit simulation. Circuit simulators convert circuits into s-domain models and solve them numerically. Search terms: transfer function, pole-zero map, region of convergence, s-plane. Newer curricula connect the ROC to causal and stable system design in control and signal processing.
